title: Are you against learning to code?
author: TaylorCooper337
selftext: I think more people getting into coding is awesome and empowering, even just vibe-coding where you don't know what's going on. But you should 100% be reading your code and trying to understand/learn it. You can learn really fast if you pay attention and actually read your code (probably much faster than traditional methods.) I've had people tell me I'm anti for saying people should still learn code and it can only help you get better at prompting even if that's all you plan on doing. Am I alone?

If you don't know, you put a lot of responsibility on the LLM to understand the hidden nuance of what you're asking.  
If you do know, it won't guess at anything. You can speak in very specific ways and get much more accurate results for things.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
As someone who's been coding for 20 years, I think the people who refuse to will find the limitations of AI coding after a while. With art, we can look at it and see bad elements. If you're not looking at code, you won't see that. 

But for small projects, small games, they're not too likely to run into those issues. I think it can work for people. For instance, some of the tools I've written I haven't checked the code for. They're too simple, serving a specific purpose. Set and forget. I can see the argument for not bothering to check the code on those. For instance, I haven't bothered checking the code for a few tools I wrote to combine images and prompts with my predefined data. Or for the simple command line tools I wrote to work with JSON data. 

It just isn't worth my time to check, it either works or it doesn't, and it's not exposed to users. Mostly all I'd be learning is the specific way it parses command line arguments. 

So I can see where pure vibe coders are coming from. I can see that if they're not willing to learn, there will be an upper limit to what they can achieve before the code gets too tangled and complex for any AI to work on. In a similar way that my AI artwork and models have a definitive upper limit on what I can achieve without learning all the nuances of modelling. 

But it works well enough for my needs, and I am learning Blender slowly. But I am happy enough with what I can craft from detailed style guidelines and specific ship descriptions. 

People have different priorities, and different ways of understanding. I definitely think it's a good idea to learn as much as you can, but some people are happy with what works for now. Maybe later on when they run into difficulties having AI vibe it all for them they'll take the time to sit down and learn what's going on. But it could take time to get there.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
And even if you want to get into low level stuff like writing a compiler and in assembly, there's just so much of the modern tools you lose. I wrote an OS for a tiny virtual machine, without AI - it's taken me years and it has bugs I've never been able to rectify. Not having useful valgrind output (it's a vm), difficulties debugging (no debugger unless you want to step through the assembled instructions individually), and simple mistakes. 

I had Claude look over it and it's already solved a few issues I just hadn't noticed - like releasing memory I'm still using. It just all got so big and complicated I struggled to see simple flows. Or the complex ones that only happen under certain conditions (interrupts are a pain.) 

So even if you *are* doing that low level stuff, AI agents are still useful. Because of how complex everything is at those levels.

comments.author: k4b0b
comments.body:
Not stricly necessary to understand code going forward, but understanding it (and more importantly the actual concepts behind it) can give you an unfair advantage.

AI will meet your bar for quality. If you don’t know what great looks like, you won’t get the _best_ results.

Now, do you care about getting the _best_ results? That depends. Probably not for small prototypes, hobby projects, or even certain professional settings.

It’s like any other part of the creation process. AI compounds your strengths and gives you a baseline for your weaknesses. Is having the best code important for your game? Or are you better off investing that time building your other skills? Depends on your goals.

As someone who’s been coding for 25+ years, I’d say the models will keep getting better and producing better code, and over time developers will care less about the code and more about the end product (that’s already the case in a lot of places). It’s happened with other parts of the tech stack as we move up the value chain.
